Introduction

  • Preoperative assessment is fundamental to achieve good surgical outcomes.
  • Consider if the patient is medically fit to undergo the proposed procedure.
  • The benefits of the surgery outweigh the potential risks.
  • May take place in a dedicated assessment clinic a few weeks before surgery.
  • Allows to admit the patient hospital on the day prior or on the actual day of surgery.

PRESENTATION TITLE

2

Speaker notes

careful preoperative assessment is fundamental to achieve good surgical outcomes

the surgeon should consider whether the patient is medically fit enough to undergo the proposed procedure and if the benefits of the surgery outweigh the potential risks and severity of any complications

Preoperative assessment may take place in a dedicated assessment clinic a few weeks before surgery and culminates in the admission to hospital on the preceding day or, more usually, on the actual day of surgery

Notes

Purpose & Scope

DEFINITION
Preoperative assessment = pre-procedure assessment, not limited to surgery — applies to any invasive procedure (e.g. GI endoscopy, interventional radiology/endovascular procedures). Goals: provide the best possible treatment, minimize preventable complications/errors, and determine whether the procedure is appropriate and safe.

Notes

1. History & Physical Examination

FIRST & CRUCIAL STEP
Establish the presenting problem/diagnosis, past medical history, past surgical/anesthetic history, and current functional/medical status.

Comorbidities may require optimization before elective surgery — e.g. a patient needing cholecystectomy with uncontrolled diabetes: control glucose first, then operate; operating with severe hyperglycemia increases complications.

WHY PRIOR ANESTHETIC HISTORY MATTERS
Previous surgery/anesthesia may reveal preventable risks: prior anaphylaxis to anesthetic/medication, or previous surgical/anesthetic complications. Identify these beforehand to prevent recurrence.
  • Family history of malignant hyperthermia → avoid the triggers: depolarizing muscle relaxants (succinylcholine) AND volatile anesthetic agents (use TIVA); dantrolene is the treatment, not the prevention. 442
  • HbA1c 14 before elective cosmetic breast reduction → agree with the surgeon who refused: uncontrolled diabetes = high risk (ASA 3); optimize first. 436
  • Who needs a pre-op ECG? The older patient — e.g. 60-year-old for elective lap cholecystectomy (not the 22-year-old for breast implants). 441

-CVS: The severity of cardiovascular disease should be assessed and signs

of undiagnosed or inadequately treated disease sought. A full history

should include exercise tolerance, existing cardiovascular disease or

risk factors (e.g., hypertension) and symptoms associated with cardiovascular

disease (e.g., chest pain, intermittent claudication, or

syncope). A history of angina and previous myocardial infarction

(MI) may indicate significant coronary artery disease. Patients may

have undergone percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI), e.g.,

angioplasty, stenting or cardiac surgery, e.g., valve surgery or bypass

grafting. Shortness of breath on exercise (exertional dyspnoea),

lying flat (orthopnoea) and waking from sleep (paroxysmal nocturnal

dyspnoea) may indicate left ventricular failure, whereas significant

dependent oedema could signify right-sided

heart failure.

Drug history may alert to the presence and severity of cardiovascular

disease. Blackouts and dizzy spells may be a sign of arrhythmias,

valvular heart or cerebrovascular disease. Clinical examination

should detect arrhythmias, heart murmurs, hypertension and signs

of cardiac failure. New or worsening symptoms should be assessed

where possible prior to surgery. Antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants

are widely prescribed in the general population, and these or

other cardiovascular medications may need to be stopped or modified

prior to surgery. Formal assessment of cardiovascular status,

e.g., using cardiopulmonary exercise testing, may be undertaken in

certain patient groups (see following section).

Respiratory system

A history of new or increased cough, sputum production and shortness

of breath or wheeze may indicate previously undiagnosed respiratory

disease or an exacerbation of preexisting pulmonary disease. In

patients with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

or fibrotic lung disease, purulent sputum may indicate an infective

exacerbation. In asthmatics, previous intensive care unit (ICU) and

hospital admissions, as well as steroid dependency, indicate severe

disease. Functional respiratory reserve is best assessed by exercise

tolerance, for example, by how far a patient can walk on the flat, up

an incline, or how many stairs they can climb before needing to rest

because of shortness of breath. Significant dyspnoea should be investigated

with pulmonary function tests.

Patients with acute respiratory illness should have surgery postponed

where possible due to the increased risk of bronchospasm and

susceptibility of the respiratory epithelium to postoperative bacterial

pneumonia. General anaesthesia exacerbates the problems by

depressing ciliary

Medications

  • Long-term steroid therapy
  • Antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulants
  • Oral contraceptives and hormone-replacement therapy
  • Psychiatric drugs
  • Diabetes

- Psych: Concurrent use of serotonin-selective

reuptake

inhibitors (SSRIs), lithium, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)

and tricyclic antidepressants has implications for general anaesthesia.

There is a risk of serotonin syndrome if SSRIs are given concurrently

with tramadol. There is also an increased risk of bleeding if

kidneys, so it may accumulate in renal dysfunction and also inter

act

with anaesthetic agents and muscle relaxants. Side effects include

arrhythmias and gastrointestinal disturbance. It is not essential that

tricyclic antidepressants be stopped preoperatively, but the anaesthe

tist

should be alerted as they may cause hypotension and arrhythmia.

MAOIs are now seldom used but interact with opiates and vasopressor

agents with the potential of neurologic and cardiovascular complica

tions.

Ideally, they should be stopped 2 to 3 weeks prior to surgery but

in an emergency, opiates and pressor agents should be avoided.

  • Pregnancy: the second trimester is the safest time for (non-urgent) surgery. 437

Investigations: Patient vs. Surgery Risk

Speaker notes

For many patients in good health undergoing relatively mild surgery,

preoperative investigations are not required. For those with more

severe comorbidities or who are undergoing major surgery, full blood

count, coagulation screen, urea and electrolytes, electrocardiograph

(ECG) or tests of respiratory function may be needed

Women of child-bearing

age should be asked if they might be pregnant

and a pregnancy test carried out. Patients with a family history of sickle

cell disease or sickle trait may require testing for this disease.

Assessment of functional status has been part of

routine preoperative history taking for many years, and self-reported

poor exercise tolerance has been shown to correlate with increased

perioperative risk.

Pre-hab

  • Undergoing a major surgical procedure is associated with significant physiologic stress.
  • Increasing functional capacity prior to surgery is associated with better outcomes.
  • Particular relevance to older patients.

The earlier version of this lecture — Dr. Abobotain's notes were written from it.

History & Physical

  • First step in any pre-op assessment.
  • Must include past medical & surgical histories.
  • Verify indications for surgery.
  • Rule out contraindications for surgery.
  • Review recent investigations and order other if needed.
SituationWhat to do
Short course in the past (e.g. prednisone 3 days, 2 months ago)No extra supplementation 439
On steroids + minor surgery (e.g. inguinal hernia, prednisolone 10 mg)Continue usual dose, no supplement 441
On steroids + moderate surgery (e.g. total knee replacement)Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction, then 25 mg q8h for 24 h 437 ×2
On steroids + major surgery (e.g. thoracic)Usual morning dose + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 50 mg q8h 442
  • Child-Pugh A → anticipated surgical mortality < 10% (B ≈ 30%, C ≈ 80%). 437
Notes

2. Verify the Indication for Surgery/Procedure

Does the patient actually need surgery?
What is the indication?
Are there non-operative/alternative treatments?
Are there any contraindications?
KEY PRINCIPLE
Being technically able to operate ≠ operation is necessary or best. Some patients can undergo surgery but should not, because risk/benefit favors another option. Review all previous investigations (MRI, CT, etc.) personally and add further investigations if needed — do not rely solely on another clinician's conclusion.

Pre-op Testing

  • General blood tests (e.g. PTT/INR, CBC, Chem, HCG).
  • Specific blood tests (e.g. LFTs, tumor markers, hormonal profiles).
  • Imaging (e.g. X-rays, CT, MRI, etc).
  • Type & screen/crossmatch.
  • Glucose and HBA1c for diabetic patients.
Notes

3. Preoperative Investigations

General Laboratory Tests

TestPurpose / Notes
CBCEnsure adequate Hb/blood counts — undiagnosed anemia is important, especially before procedures with expected significant blood loss
Coagulation profile (INR/PTT)Identify anticoagulation/coagulopathy even before apparently minor procedures — a missed abnormality can cause major bleeding even in a "small" procedure
Chemistry/electrolytesIdentify electrolyte/metabolic abnormalities
Pregnancy testingIn patients of childbearing potential when appropriate — affects anesthesia and procedure urgency; ask whether the procedure can safely wait
COAGULATION — DO NOT ASSUME "MINOR"
Check coagulation broadly rather than assuming a small procedure is harmless. Rare severe maternal situations may require pregnancy termination to save the mother.
Notes

Procedure-/Disease-Specific Blood Tests

Order tests relevant to the disease/procedure — e.g. liver surgery → liver function assessment.

TUMOR MARKERS
May be diagnostic, prognostic, or a baseline for postoperative surveillance.
Prostate cancer → PSA: baseline before treatment; post-resection decline assesses response; later rise may indicate recurrence.
Pituitary tumors → hormonal assessment: helps diagnosis/classification, may determine treatment, useful for follow-up.
EXAMPLE — PROLACTINOMA
Pituitary mass + high prolactin consistent with prolactinoma → usually medical treatment rather than surgery. Serial prolactin levels monitor response/recurrence.
  • Child-Pugh uses albumin, total bilirubin, INR/PT, ascites, encephalopathy (not platelets). 436 ×2
Notes

4. Imaging

Obtain imaging appropriate to the anatomy/pathology being treated — e.g. orthopedic fracture/joint replacement → X-ray ± further imaging; depending on condition → CT, MRI, specialized imaging, MRCP, etc. Imaging should define the relevant anatomy and pathology before intervention.

Notes

5. Blood Availability

RULE OF THUMB
Ensure appropriate type and screen ± cross-match. Not every procedure requires cross-matched blood, but unexpected vascular injury/major bleeding can occur even during apparently minor procedures — have at least type and screen ready before any intervention where bleeding could become significant.
Notes

6. Glycemic Assessment

WHY IT MATTERS
Glucose + HbA1c are particularly important because diabetes is common and substantially affects perioperative risk. Poor glycemic control may cause infection, metabolic/acidosis complications, or diabetic emergencies/coma. Elective surgery may need delay until diabetes is adequately controlled.
  • Well-controlled asthmatic having an emergency appendectomy → ASA 2E (add "E" for emergency). 431
  • Hypothyroid patient for elective lap chole → reschedule until euthyroid (risk of myxedema coma after surgery in hypothyroid patients). 438 ×2 438
  • Tight glucose control decreases the incidence of deep wound infection. 438
  • Emergency (ruptured ectopic) in a diabetic with glucose 13 mmol/L → operate without further investigation; don't delay a life-threatening emergency for ECG/CXR/consults. 430

Risk Assessment

Cardiac assessment

  • ECG =/- echo, stress testing, blood tests (e.g. creatinine level).
  • Assess perioperative MI risk.
  • Risk factors such as age, smoking, CHF, lung and kidney disease.
  • Optimize cardiac function pre-op, modify risk factors.
  • Who needs an extensive pre-op assessment? The patient with significant uncontrolled disease, e.g. 60-year-old with atrial fibrillation + uncontrolled CHF — not the healthy young patient or the patient having a skin excision under local. 442
Notes

7. Perioperative Risk Assessment

After confirming indication and completing history, examination, and investigations, determine the risk of operating on this specific patient. Being a surgical candidate only means the patient can undergo surgery — the decision still depends on whether surgery is necessary, benefit exceeds risk, and risk can be reduced/optimized.

Notes

ASA Physical Status Classification

Most commonly used general perioperative risk classification: ASA = American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status.
ClassDescription
ASA IHealthy patient, no systemic disease — uncommon before disease-related surgery, more likely in elective/cosmetic procedures
ASA IIMild systemic disease without significant functional limitation
ASA IIISevere systemic disease with functional limitation, but not a constant/immediate threat to life
ASA IVSevere systemic disease that is a constant threat to life — e.g. end-stage liver failure or severe heart failure awaiting transplant
ASA VMoribund patient unlikely to survive without the operation — e.g. severe trauma with life-threatening head injury or active intra-abdominal hemorrhage requiring immediate surgery
ASA VIBrain-dead patient undergoing organ donation — a donor classified ASA VI may donate to a critically ill transplant recipient
  • Smoker with well-controlled hypertension, no end-organ damage → ASA II. 442 ×2
Notes

8. Cardiac Risk Assessment

Assess cardiac status even when overt cardiac disease is not known — occult disease/arrhythmias may become clinically significant under anesthesia. Obtain at least an ECG as part of cardiac assessment, particularly when risk factors are present; further testing (echocardiography, stress testing, other specialized investigations) depends on findings/risk.

PERIOPERATIVE MI RISK
Surgery produces a physiologic stress/trauma response → ↑ cortisol + catecholamines/epinephrine → increased cardiac workload and MI risk. MI may therefore occur hours or even a day after an otherwise technically successful operation.
  • Metabolic (stress) response to surgery is reduced by a laparoscopic approach (less tissue trauma); longer operations and prolonged fasting make it worse. 438 Final
Notes

Major Risk Factors / Comorbidities

Age (non-modifiable)
Smoking (modifiable)
Heart failure/cardiovascular disease
Lung disease
Kidney disease
Diabetes and other systemic comorbidities
Notes

Smoking

Heavy smokers may benefit from delaying elective surgery when clinically possible — professor gave ~6 weeks smoking cessation as an example. Smoking increases risk of MI, stroke, surgical-site/wound infection, poor wound healing, and wound dehiscence.
  • Stop smoking 4–6 weeks before surgery — the best way to prevent post-op pulmonary complications in a smoker (6 weeks before lung surgery). 442 441 441 437
  • Elective plastic surgery: the history item that affects the surgical result is smoking (poor flap/wound healing). 437 Final
Notes

Cardiac Optimization

High-risk cardiac patients may need cardiology assessment/optimization before surgery. If surgery can safely wait, optimize cardiac function first.

Medication assessment

  • Discontinue ASA/ACs ahead of time.
  • Surgery specific meds may need to be stopped (e.g. AEDs).
  • Continue BP, DM and other meds even when NPO.
  • Warfarin: stop 5 days before surgery and bridge with LMWH (high thrombotic risk, e.g. AF). Older keys say "1 week" — same idea: stop it ahead, don't continue it and don't give vitamin K for elective surgery. 442 441 437 436 ×2
  • Therapeutic LMWH: stop 24 hours before surgery. 442
  • Drugs to continue: statin and beta-blocker (ACEI/ARB are often held the morning of surgery; warfarin is stopped). 441
  • Insulin: hold rapid-acting insulin from midnight before surgery (when NPO). 437
Notes

9. Medication Review

ALWAYS OBTAIN A COMPLETE MEDICATION HISTORY
Particularly identify anticoagulants/antiplatelets such as aspirin, warfarin, and DOACs/NOACs. Surgery may sometimes proceed while these medications are being taken, but the team must know beforehand — different agents require different pre- and postoperative interruption windows.
Notes

Procedure-Specific Medication Adjustment

Some medications must be modified because they interfere with the planned procedure — e.g. epilepsy surgery requiring intraoperative EEG localization: antiepileptic medications may need to be withheld because they can suppress/blunt EEG activity and obscure the epileptic focus being targeted.

Blood-pressure/diabetes medications are generally continued in many patients even when NPO, depending on the perioperative plan.

Disease specific assessment

  • Patient candidacy for treatment.
  • Required pre-op testing.
  • Availability of required resources.
  • Alternative options.
Notes

10. Disease-/Procedure-Specific Assessment

Determine whether the patient is a candidate for this particular treatment, not merely whether they can tolerate surgery — many diseases have several valid treatment modalities.

EXAMPLE — BRAIN METASTASIS
May be treated with surgery, radiation, or systemic medical therapy. Choose the option best suited to the specific patient. Ensure all required pre-op testing is complete; obtain anything missing.
Notes

Resource Availability

DO NOT PROCEED WITHOUT RESOURCES
Do not perform a procedure if essential resources are unavailable, even if the patient is otherwise ready — required resources may include specialized equipment/devices, specific personnel/expertise, or neurophysiology monitoring/another specialty service. If unavailable, refer/transfer the patient to a center that has them.
Notes

Alternatives

Always consider and discuss alternative management options. Explain all reasonable options and which is considered best; the final choice belongs to the appropriately informed patient.

  • Final version: Child-Pugh A cirrhosis with sigmoid cancer → mortality if operated < 10%. 437 Final

Informed Consent

  • A process by which a patient is informed of:
  • Their medical condition.
  • Treatment options with descriptions and advantages and disadvantages of each.
  • Any possible complications.
  • Expected outcome.
  • Patients agree or refuse a specific treatment.
  • Competence and ability to make decisions are crucial, otherwise a surrogate decision-maker is required.
  • Implied consent in certain situations.
Notes

11. Informed Consent

EXTREMELY IMPORTANT COMPONENT
The patient must be informed about: diagnosis, all treatment options, no treatment/observation as a legitimate option, the proposed procedure, possible complications, and expected outcome. A competent patient may choose not to receive treatment even when the condition is treatable — this decision must be respected.
  • Informed consent includes the name of the responsible surgeon (plus diagnosis, procedure, complications, prognosis, other options; the patient can change his mind at any time). 435
Notes

Complications

Discuss all relevant potential complications, including rare/uncommon complications, so unexpected outcomes are not completely unknown to the patient beforehand.

Notes

Expected Outcome / Managing Expectations

Clearly explain what the procedure is realistically expected to achieve.
Example: decompressive craniotomy after severe stroke may be performed to save life, not necessarily reverse existing paralysis. Example: spine surgery does not necessarily mean immediate postoperative walking/full neurological recovery.
Expected outcome may influence whether the patient accepts or declines surgery.
Notes

12. Capacity/Competence to Consent

The patient must be able to understand the information and make an informed decision. Patients who may lack capacity include: confused patients, reduced level of consciousness, young children, and severe dementia/Alzheimer disease.

IF CAPACITY IS UNCERTAIN
Explain the information, then ask the patient to repeat back what they understood.
  • A competent 55-year-old whose son came to sign for him → the patient himself must sign. 437 ×2
Notes

Surrogate Decision-Maker

If the patient lacks decision-making capacity, identify an appropriate surrogate able to decide on the patient's behalf — an appropriate family member, spouse, or other legally/ethically accepted surrogate.

Notes

13. Implied Consent in Emergencies

DEFINITION
Emergency treatment proceeds when the incapacitated patient cannot consent, no surrogate is available, and clinicians reasonably believe the patient would want life-saving treatment.

Example: a previously healthy 19-year-old with severe head trauma, unconscious and actively dying, with nobody available to consent → treatment can proceed.

More complicated when prior wishes/comorbidities make treatment preference uncertain — e.g. an elderly patient with advanced metastatic cancer. Implied-consent decisions commonly require agreement by two physicians that the patient would most likely consent if able.

  • Life-threatening emergency with no family available → operate; no consent needed (implied consent). 442 441 438 ×2

Infection Prevention

  • Pre-op glycemic control.
  • Nutritional status.
  • Immunocompetence assessment.
  • Pre-incision antibiotics, repeat intra-op dosing.
  • Adequate sterilization.
  • Severe COPD (SpO₂ 88%) before abdominal surgery → the most effective way to prevent post-op respiratory failure is effective pain control + incentive spirometry. 442
Notes

14. Surgical-Site Infection Prevention

Optimize Patient Risk Factors

Glycemic control — uncontrolled diabetes increases infection risk
Hypertension/vascular disease
Significant systemic medical disease
Malnutrition/emaciation (↑ risk)
Morbid obesity (↑ risk)
ASSESS IMMUNE COMPETENCE
Poorly controlled diabetes, medical comorbidities, primary immune deficiencies, and acquired immunodeficiency/immunosuppression.
Notes

Antibiotic Prophylaxis

Give pre-incision prophylactic antibiotics for most operative procedures when indicated. Re-dose approximately every 4 hours during prolonged surgery. Appropriate prophylactic antibiotics reduce surgical-site infection risk.
  • Uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy → peri-operative ceftriaxone + metronidazole (no 72-hour course). 439
  • Elective splenectomy: give the vaccines against encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae) 2–3 weeks before the operation (emergency splenectomy → ~2 weeks after). 437 Final ×2
Notes

Sterilization

Ensure the operating environment is appropriately clean, instruments are properly sterilized, and the degree of contamination/sterility is considered according to procedure type.

Notes

Specialty Examples

SpecialtyConsideration
NeurosurgeryGenerally clean wounds except procedures involving infected sites or entry through colonized mucosa (e.g. transnasal/transoral) — infection may lead to meningitis → potentially fatal
OrthopedicsDeep infection may cause osteomyelitis, potentially severe enough to require amputation
Bowel surgery / some ENT proceduresGreater exposure to normal flora — less inherently clean than standard neurosurgical procedures
UNIVERSAL RULE
Required sterility standards depend on the surgical field, but correct OR/instrument sterilization is essential in all cases.
  • Wrong knee listed and site not yet marked → time-out / verification with the team and the patient, then mark the correct site. 442
Notes

4 Have at least a type and screen ready before any procedure where bleeding could become significant

Pre-operative Assessment

History and Physical Examination:
  • Obtain patient history with mnemonic “OPQRST”:
  • O: Onset (gradual vs sudden)
  • P: Precipitant (food or movement)
  • Q: Quality (Sharp, dull, cramps)
  • R: Radiation (Back)
  • S: Stop (what offers relief)
  • T: Temporal (Duration)
  • The presence of fever, sweats, or chills usually indicates acute infection, whereas weight loss indicates a chronic condition like tumors.
  • Past medical Hx should include:
  • Prior operations
  • Prior VTE (DVT + PE)
  • Bleeding diatheses
  • Airway problems (anesthesia problems)
  • Active medications
  • Steroid use in the last 6 months (risk of adrenal insufficiency post- operatively)
  • Allergies (egg allergy leading to insecurity with propofol use and iodine use with shellfish allergy)
  • Social Hx should include alcohol, smoking, and illicit drug use
  • Family Hx should include problems related to the patient’s presentation
  • Example: colorectal cancer to test for familial conditions
  • Also check for coagulation, bleeding, and anesthesia problems
  • Example: death of a young patient in the OR might indicate an endocrine problem like pheochromocytoma
  • Also, check for systemic review
  • Obtain patient vital signs along with height, weight, and BMI
Pre-op Testing:
  • Generally, children uncommonly require preoperative lab tests for most operations. On the other hand, a complete blood count, chemistries, and electrocardiogram are proper for higher-risk patients before complex operations
  • A coagulation profile is warranted in most procedures. Conditions include:
  • Brain, spine, and neck surgeries
  • Bile duct obstruction, malnutrition, and absent terminal ileum (Vit K)
  • Pregnancy test for women of childbearing age (Beta-HCG), and blood preparation for transfusion
  • Check patient blood sugar levels as they are correlated with surgical site infections (SSIs)
  • Screen for staph aureus through nasal swabs to guide the decontamination process. MRSA screening is indicated in:
  • Immunocompromised patients
  • Open cardiac surgeries
  • Foreign bodies implantation in orthopedics and neurosurgery
  • Electrocardiograms are indicated in:
  • Older than 50
  • Vascular operations
  • Hx of hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, severe pulmonary disease, or renal dysfunction
  • Chest radiographs are indicated in suspicion of malignancy or pulmonary disease
  • Carotid US is indicated in:
  • Carotid bruits
  • Hx of cerebrovascular accident
  • Hx of transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)
  • Non-invasive venous studies are indicated in patients with prolonged immobility and/or hospital stay prior to surgery
Pre-op Process:

1- Risk Assessment and Reduction

  • Essentially based on the ASA score
  • The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) has the following factors for cardiac complications:
  • Hx of ischemic heart disease
  • Congestive heart failure
  • Cerebrovascular disease
  • High-risk operation
  • Pre-op treatment with insulin
  • Pre-op Creatinine of > 2 mg/dl
  • Additional risk factors include:
  • Old age
  • Smoking
  • Insulin-dependent diabetes
  • Coronary artery disease
  • Abnormal cardiac stress test
  • long-term beta-blocker therapy
  • COPD
  • creatinine of > or equal to 1.8 mg/dl
  • Noninvasive stress testing before noncardiac operations is indicated in:
  • Patients with active cardiac conditions (unstable angina, recent MI, significant arrhythmias, or severe valve disease)
  • Patients who require vascular operations and have clinical risk factors and poor functional capacity
  • coronary revascularization before non-cardiac operations is indicated in:
  • Significant left main coronary artery stenosis
  • Stable angina with three-vessel disease
  • Stable angina with two-vessel disease and significant LAD coronary artery stenosis with either an ejection fraction < 50% or ischemia on noninvasive testing
  • High-risk unstable angina
  • Non-ST-segment elevation Ml
  • Acute ST-elevation MI
  • Beta-blockers should be continued among those patients who are already taking them and among those having a vascular operation and at high cardiac risk, including known coronary heart disease or the presence of ischemia preoperative testing
  • Preoperative aspirin usage should continue among patients at moderate to high risk for coronary artery disease unless the risk of resultant bleeding outweighs the likelihood of an atherothrombotic event
  • Thienopyridines, such as ticlopidine or clopidogrel, are administered in concert with aspirin as dual antiplatelet therapy following the placement of coronary artery stents
  • Elective operations with a significant risk of bleeding should be delayed 12 months before the discontinuation of the thienopyridine in the presence of a drug-eluting stent, at least 4-6 weeks for bare-metal stents, and 4 weeks after balloon angioplasty
  • Postoperative pulmonary complications (PCCs) have risk factors:
  • Old age
  • High ASA score
  • Congestive heart failure
  • COPD
  • Altered mental status, alcohol, and malnutrition
  • OSA (use STOP-BANG questionnaire to screen)
  • It is recommended to stop smoking at least 4 weeks before surgery (4-6 weeks is acceptable)
  • Pulmonary function tests and baseline arterial blood gas tests guide the care of selected patients, especially those anticipating lung resection. In addition, asthma should be medically controlled
  • The efficacy of stockings for VTE prevention is unproven. This can violate skin integrity and result in the accumulation of edema. A 4-week course of LMWH is recommended, especially in abdominal or pelvic malignancies
  • An extended duration of outpatient prophylaxis with enoxaparin after operations for cancer resulted in a statistically significant reduction in VTE events, compared with inpatient administration only, with no increase in bleeding complications. Therefore, prophylaxis should be maintained after the discharge of patients who have elevated risk scores
  • The relative risk of an SSI seems to increase incrementally in a linear pattern with the degree of hyperglycemia with glucose levels > 140 mg/dl
  • Glucose levels of 181-300 mg/dl prompt the need to begin an infusion of IV insulin before the operation, along with a 5% dextrose solution to minimize the chances of hypoglycemia
  • Patients with glucose levels of > 300 mg/dL are assessed for ketones or acidosis prior to starting an insulin infusion
  • Intravenous insulin is best for perioperative glucose control due to its rapid onset of action, short half-life, and Immediate availability
  • Antibiotics should be administered 1 hour before incision. Additional doses are administered after two-half lives during the operation (4 hours for cefazolin)
  • 1st generation cephalosporins are preferred (Clindamycin if penicillin- allergic)
  • 2nd generation cephalosporins to cover gram -ve and anaerobes (could give 1st generation + metronidazole)
  • When antibiotics are administered for SSI prophylaxis rather than for treatment of an established or suspected infection, they are typically not continued after surgery, except in special circumstances such as vascular grafts, cardiac surgery, or joint replacements
  • The maintenance of perioperative normothermia also has salutary effects on wound oxygen tension levels and can consequently reduce the incidence of SSIs
  • Some data support hyperoxygenation with FiO2 >= 80% during the first 2 hours after a major colorectal surgery. In addition, protocols with mupirocin nasal ointment application and chlorhexidine soap showers have reduced the incidence of SSIs among patients colonized with methicillin- sensitive S aureus
Fluid Management and Blood Volume:
  • Pulmonary artery catheterization is associated with increased mortality rates. It may be considered in selected cases who show clinical cardiac instability with comorbid conditions
  • Dialysis should be performed within about 24-36 hours before an operation to avoid electrolyte disturbances after conferring with a nephrologist
  • Blood transfusions are indicated in cases of blood diatheses after conferring with a hematologist. Since these were found to be associated with high mortality rates, it’s crucial to weigh the benefits and risks
Nutrition:
  • Hypo-albuminemia (albumin < 3.0 mg/dl) is an independent risk factor for the development of SSIs, with a fivefold increased incidence compared to a normal patient.
  • The obesity surgery mortality score for gastric bypass (poor prognosis):
  • BMI >= 50
  • Male sex
  • Hypertension
  • PE risks (Past Hx, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension)
  • Age >= 45
Endocrine:
  • Steroid use should not be done indiscriminately as this increases the risk of infections
  • Thyrotoxicosis should be corrected to avoid thyroid storm:
    • Antithyroid medications (propylthiouracil or methimazole)
    • Beta-blockers and corticosteroids
    • Saturated solution of potassium iodide
  • Hypothyroidism can progress to hypothermia and hemodynamic collapse, so treat with:
    • Hormone replacement (Levothyroxine)
  • CT with contrast should be avoided with goiter patients as this may exacerbate the condition (iodine contrast)
Illicit drugs and alcohol:
  • In general, patients should refrain from illicit drugs for at least 2 weeks before the surgery. They should also refrain from alcohol at least 1 week before the surgery
  • Give benzodiazepines to control the withdrawal symptoms
Cancer Therapy:
  • It is recommended to have at least 4-6 weeks between bevacizumab and an operation, and therapy should not resume until after 4 weeks when the wound heals
Informed Consent:
  • A process by which the patient is informed of their medical condition, treatment options, possible complications, and expected outcomes
  • Patient capacity should be taken into consideration with making decisions. A health proxy should be sorted in case the patient is incapacitated
Preoperative Instructions:
  • Refraining from food/drinks before anesthesia:
    • Liquids: 2 hours
    • Breast milk for infants: 4 hours
    • Formula milk for infants: 6 hours
    • Light meals: 6 hours
    • Fatty meals: 8 hours
  • Patient medications are generally continued until the morning of the surgery. Chronic narcotics, for example, are continued on the day of surgery to avoid withdrawal symptoms
  • NSAIDs, herbal preparations, and vitamin E can disrupt normal coagulation and should be stopped 1 week before an operation
  • Estrogen receptor antagonist (Tamoxifen) should be stopped 2-4 weeks before an operation
  • Stopping Warfarin 5 days before surgery results in the normalization of the INR, and the surgeon will decide if a bridge therapy is required or not
  • DOACs should be stopped 48 hours before the scheduled procedure
Operating room:
  • Local clippers are used to remove hair in the OR. Razors should be avoided due to the risk of infection
  • The addition of isopropyl alcohol to chlorhexidine provides the best outcome in skin preparations
